title: I used a wheelchair for the first time in hospital, then built a racing game out of it with Claude
author: office-canard
selftext:
In August I spent about three weeks in hospital and used a wheelchair for the first time. What surprised me was how interesting it was to drive. Each hand moves one wheel. Push both to go straight, ease off one side to turn, pull one back to spin on the spot.



I kept thinking it would make a great racing game, so I made one.



WHEELCHAIR D gives each wheel its own lever: left thumb for the left wheel, right thumb for the right.



\- 31 courses, from circuits to point-to-point street runs

\- Time trial with world records

\- Battle mode against three rivals

\- Rain and dirt conditions



How AI fit in: I built it with Claude. I described how a real wheelchair feels to push, and Claude wrote the code. Most of my own time went into driving it over and over and saying what felt wrong. The idea and the feel came from my hospital stay. The code came from Claude.



I'm a one-person studio, and this is one of 23 small games I've released so far. I'd love to hear what you think of the controls. Does it click right away, or does it take a few runs?

comments.author: Forward_Toe4409
comments.body: was it created with unity or another tech?

replies.author: office-canard
replies.body: No engine. It's plain JavaScript with three.js, wrapped as a mobile app with Capacitor. Claude writes the code, so I never needed an engine.

replies.author: Fuzzzy420
replies.body:
Sorry,  have to correct you just for the sake of others reading it. 

Three js is your engine and you don't use plain js since you use three.js. Even without three.js you would need an engine which ai would build for you. 

Lastly capacitor was not build for games, the more stuff you add the more problems you will get with performance. Capacitor is a web viewer first. 

My recommendation: now you know that you like the idea, build it in godot/ unity you will save yourself so much trouble in the long run. 

I'm happy to get corrected here.

replies.author: office-canard
replies.body: Fair point, thanks. You're right that three.js is doing the engine's job here, so "no engine" wasn't the best way to put it. And yes, Capacitor is a web view first. For small games like mine it's been working out so far, and when something gets heavy I trim it down. If one of them ever grows into something bigger, Godot would definitely be worth a look.

comments.author: No-Range139
comments.body: Did Claude get the models somewhere and maps or was this all created in threejs or elsewhere?

replies.author: office-canard
replies.body: The characters and their animations are from Mixamo. It happened to have a wheelchair animation, which was perfect. The wheelchair model is a free asset. For the courses, I started from real circuits, and the mountain passes came from real terrain data that I simplified. But once I tuned them to how a wheelchair actually handles, they ended up looking nothing like the originals.

comments.body: This is actually a really cool game because ableism ignores ppl using wheelchairs. My dad was one from 30-60. A lot of kids play basketball in wheelchairs, adults too. I’m really sure they would actually be happy youe are representing them

replies.author: office-canard
replies.body:
Thank you for sharing about your dad.



I'm Japanese, and I think the West is much more open to wheelchair users than Japan is.



When I started making this game, I was surprised that Mixamo actually had wheelchair animations. You might not believe this, but if a Japanese 3D asset supplier made wheelchair animations, I'm pretty sure there'd be an uproar: "That's discrimination. Are you turning wheelchair users into a toy?"



Discrimination is always close to us. But it's the best when there's something everyone can enjoy together, whatever their situation.
